title: Categorical Completeness and Type-Level Invariants of Bitmapped Vector Tries in Idris 2
abstract: Persistent random-access sequences are typically implemented using either balanced trees, incurring logarithmic overhead per operation, or bitmapped vector tries (BVTs), which achieve near-constant amortised performance through wide branching but traditionally rely on runtime bounds checks to guarantee structural safety. This paper presents a formally verified implementation of the 32-way Bitmapped Vector Trie in Idris 2, in which five core structural invariants -- depth-uniformity, fixed branching factor, bounded bitwise indexing, exhaustive pattern matching, and length-indexed buffering -- are encoded directly in dependent types and checked at compile time. We further establish a lawful Monad instance via an induced structure over the canonical list isomorphism, without expanding the implementation to a fully balanced concatenation scheme such as Relaxed Radix Balanced trees. Benchmarks on a Haskell prototype against Data.Sequence and Data.IntMap confirm that the underlying algorithmic behaviour matches theoretical expectations, despite the prototype's raw performance lagging behind mature, optimised libraries.

title: Five-Step Multi-Dimensional Learnability Validation Protocol
abstract: Reference implementation of a five-step protocol that determines, before model development begins, whether a clinical prediction target is learnable from the available features, and whether a model fitted to it passes five complementary validation checks and is eligible for further validation. Version 2.0 accompanies the revised JCTA manuscript (round 2). Each step is implemented once (src/protocol.py) with all settings in src/config.py; the Step 1 rule is max |Pearson r| > 0.10 or max mutual information > 0.05, and a Step 1 failure is reported as a warning; positive classes are Bacterial, High Risk and Deceased; Step 5 requires at least 70% sign agreement; LightGBM is the representative model. Reproduce with python src/run_all.py, python src/figures.py and pytest tests.

title: TiLCA-Net: nuclei segmentation and classification in pathological images via task-specialized attention and efficient decoding
abstract: Background: Nuclei segmentation and classification in whole-slide images (WSIs) are critical for tumor diagnosis and treatment. Existing methods often face multi-task feature conflict and computational redundancy. This study aimed to develop an efficient multi-task framework that balances segmentation accuracy and inference efficiency. Methods: To seek an improved balance between segmentation accuracy and efficiency, this study proposes TiLCA-Net, a network that integrates multi-scale attention mechanisms with a lightweight decoding strategy to optimize comprehensive model performance. First, a Task-Specialized Attention Integrated Encoder (TSEncoder) is designed to decouple features by assigning spatial, global, and channel attention at multiple levels, thereby mitigating negative transfer. Second, we introduce an iterative cross-enhancement (ICE) module, which utilizes closed-loop iteration and median pooling to enhance global geometric consistency and robustness. Finally, a Lightweight Context Aggregation Decoder (LCA-Decoder) is introduced, replacing redundant structures with multi-scale aggregation to substantially reduce computational cost while preserving high-frequency details. Results: Experiments on CoNSeP, MoNuSeg, and CervCell-Seg demonstrate that TiLCA-Net achieves a favorable balance between segmentation performance and computational efficiency. TiLCA-Net achieved mean panoptic quality (PQ) scores of 0.528, 0.578, and 0.592 on CoNSeP, MoNuSeg, and CervCell-Seg, respectively, compared with 0.504, 0.563, and 0.578 for HoVer-Net. These results indicate PQ improvements of 0.024, 0.015, and 0.014 on the three datasets, respectively. Patch-level benchmarking showed that TiLCA-Net required fewer floating point operations per second (FLOPs) and achieved higher batch throughput than HoVer-Net, but with higher single-patch latency and peak graphics processing unit (GPU) memory. Conclusions: Through feature decoupling and efficient decoder reconstruction, TiLCA-Net provides a practical accuracy-efficiency trade-off for patch-level nuclei analysis in computational pathology.

title: MIMIC-Ext-SynNotes: Large-Scale Synthetic Clinical Notes via Rephrasing MIMIC-III/IV with LLMs
abstract: MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV are foundational resources for clinical NLP, but their scale is modest relative to the data volumes needed to train language models. Building on recent advances in synthetic data generation through LLM-based rephrasing, we construct **MIMIC-Ext-SynNotes** by rephrasing all clinical notes from MIMIC-III/IV with five open-weight LLMs. The release comprises eight synthetic corpora totalling **13.7B words** , roughly a tenfold expansion of the free text in MIMIC. An accompanying peer-reviewed study evaluates the corpus through intrinsic similarity analysis, downstream clinical NLP tasks, fairness assessment, LLM-based fact-checking, and human error analysis. It finds that the synthetic notes preserve core clinical information and predictive utility for coarse-grained tasks but lose fine- grained detail -- a loss largely mitigated by rephrasing in chunks rather than whole notes. We release the resource to support research in clinical language modeling, synthetic data generation, and domain adaptation for healthcare LLMs.

title: Artificial intelligence for clean technologies: a cross-sectoral review of sustainable, data-driven, and policy-aware systems
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is emerging as a cornerstone technology for accelerating the clean energy transition. Unlike incremental optimizations, AI reshapes how energy and environmental systems are designed, operated, and governed. Existing reviews typically focus on single domains such as forecasting, smart grids, or carbon capture, providing useful yet fragmented insights. This review moves beyond these silos to deliver a cross-sectoral synthesis of more than 450 studies, offering one of the most comprehensive mappings of AI in clean technologies to date. We assess applications spanning renewable energy forecasting, energy storage, hydrogen and bioenergy, carbon capture and utilization (CCUS), and recycling within circular economy pathways. We emphasize AI supports lifecycle assessment (LCA) and techno-economic analysis (TEA), linking innovation to system-level sustainability and cost-effectiveness. In addition to cataloguing technical advances, we critically examine persistent challenges: data scarcity, model interpretability, algorithmic bias, cybersecurity risks, and integration with legacy infrastructure. We also address AI’s own environmental footprint, including the energy intensity of training large-scale models, underscoring the need for sustainable digital practices. Finally, we propose a roadmap built on open datasets, physics-informed and interpretable AI models, ethical and governance frameworks, and stronger alignment between technology, policy, and markets. By unifying fragmented perspectives across sectors, this review provides researchers, industry leaders, and policymakers with actionable insights to deploy AI responsibly, positioning it as an enabler of an equitable, resilient, and sustainable clean energy future.

title: An Explainable DistilBERT-BiLSTM-Attention Framework for Binary and Multi-Class Hate Speech Detection
abstract: Hate speech on social media poses serious risks to social harmony, mental well-being, and public safety, making its timely and accurate detection essential for content moderation systems. Most existing studies focus on binary classification, evaluated their frameworks on a single dataset, and provide limited insight into how decisions are made, which limits their real-world applicability. In addition, limited work is done on the explainability of their predictive inference. To address these challenges, this study proposes a multilevel and explainable hate speech detection framework. The proposed model integrates DistilBERT (Distilled Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) embeddings with a Bi-LSTM (Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory) model, and an attention mechanism to capture both contextual meaning and sequential dependencies in text. To enhance trust and transparency, LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations) is employed to explain model predictions by highlighting influential textual features. The framework is evaluated on two benchmark datasets using both binary and multi-class classification to examine robustness and generalization. In addition, an ablation study is presented to highlight the significance of various components of proposed framework. For binary classification, the proposed model achieves F1-scores of 96.78% on the Davidson dataset and 99.53% on the SMHS dataset. In the multi-class setting, it attains F1-scores of 97.00% and 94.99% on the Davidson and SMHS datasets, respectively, outperforming existing baseline approaches. The results demonstrate that multilevel evaluation improves the reliability that the proposed framework effectively balances performance and efficiency. This makes the framework suitable for practical hate speech moderation systems that require accurate, generalizable, and explainable decisions.

In the multi-class setting, it attains F1-scores of 97.00% and 94.99% on the Davidson and SMHS datasets, respectively, outperforming existing baseline approaches. The results demonstrate that multilevel evaluation improves the reliability that the proposed framework effectively balances performance and efficiency. This makes the framework suitable for practical hate speech moderation systems that require accurate, generalizable, and explainable decisions.

title: Mizar: A 159M-Parameter Audio-Language Model for Audio Understanding
abstract: Audio-language models (ALMs) integrate acoustic perception with the knowledge encoded in language models, enabling contextual understanding of auditory events. Making these capabilities practical on devices with limited memory and computation motivates our focus on small ALMs with fewer than 200M parameters. We introduce a recipe that brings together architecture, data, and three-stage training to build Mizar, a 159.3M-parameter ALM. Its architecture connects a compact CED-Small audio encoder to SmolLM2-135M through a frequency-merging mapper. With supervision drawn from ReasonAQA, AudioMCQ, and AVQA, the model undergoes three training stages: audio-language alignment (Stage 1), audio-dependent fine-tuning (Stage 2), and post-training (Stage 3) aimed at strengthening weak skills while retaining learned capabilities. Across five random seeds, Mizar achieves mean accuracies of 52.92% on MMAU, 42.42% on MMAR, and 36.02% on ADQA-clean, surpassing the previous best-performing ALM below 200M parameters on all three benchmarks. It also supports local inference on a single CPU: on questions from the MMAU benchmark, the mean latency from opening the audio file to generating a complete answer is 1.09 seconds. Code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/KaiyangLi1992/Mizar_159M.

title: Visual Tripwires: Anticipating Failure in Deep Vision Systems
abstract: Deep vision systems remain vulnerable to corruption, occlusion, and distribution shift despite strong benchmark performance. Existing reliability methods typically evaluate uncertainty at individual time steps and do not explicitly model how a system progresses toward failure. We introduce Visual Tripwires, a predictive reliability framework that uses temporal instability in model behaviour to anticipate impending failure. Our central hypothesis is that predictive degradation develops progressively through measurable changes in latent representations, prediction trajectories, and attention structure. Visual Tripwires captures these changes using representation drift, prediction oscillation, trajectory curvature, and attention entropy. A lightweight tripwire predictor aggregates these signals over a temporal window to estimate the probability of failure within a future prediction horizon. Experiments across multiple datasets, architectures, and progressive perturbation settings show that the proposed instability signals emerge before predictive degradation and provide earlier and more accurate failure warnings than conventional uncertainty estimation methods. These results demonstrate that temporal instability contains useful information about future model reliability and provides a practical basis for early warning in deep vision systems.

title: BFI: An R Package for Bayesian Federated Inference
abstract: Bayesian Federated Inference (BFI) estimates statistical models from multicenter data when individual-level observations cannot be combined across centers. We present \pkg{BFI}, an \proglang{R} package that implements this methodology for Gaussian, binomial logistic, and survival regression models. Each center performs a Bayesian maximum a posteriori analysis and sends only parameter estimates and curvature information to a central server, where these summaries are combined to approximate the analysis of the combined data. The package supports prior specification, structured forms of between-center heterogeneity, several parametric and flexible baseline-hazard models for survival analysis, and treatment-effect estimation for observational and randomized studies. We describe the software design and the information exchanged between centers, give reproducible workflows for these analyses, and compare the federated results with pooled-data analyses for Gaussian, logistic, and survival models.

title: How to read an AI model launch announcement: six claims worth checking before you repeat them
abstract: How to read an AI model launch announcement: six claims worth checking before you repeat them Model launches arrive with the same shape every time: a benchmark chart, a few superlatives, a waitlist, and a flurry of posts that repeat the chart without opening it. We read a lot of these announcements at FuturPulse, and the same six questions do most of the work of separating signal from marketing. 1. Is the benchmark the one you actually run? A model can top a reasoning benchmark and still be the wrong choice for your workload. Benchmarks measure a task distribution chosen by whoever runs them. Before the chart changes your roadmap, find the eval that resembles your traffic — long-context extraction, tool-calling loops, multilingual support, code edits — and note whether it exists at all. "No result published on X" is a finding, not a gap to fill with optimism. 2. Compared against which version of the competitor? Benchmark comparisons are only meaningful with the exact model names, versions and settings stated. "Beats the previous generation of the leading competitor" is unfalsifiable. Look for a table, not a sentence. 3. Cloud API, weights, or neither? Three very different products hide behind one announcement: a hosted endpoint with rate limits, downloadable weights under a licence with conditions, or a demo. Each has different cost, latency and privacy consequences. If the post does not say which one, assume the most restrictive reading until the docs appear. 4. What does "available today" exclude? Regions, tiers, waitlists and preview programmes are where availability claims quietly shrink. A launch that is real for one enterprise tier and a form-fill for everyone else is not dishonest — it is just not what the headline said. 5. What changed in the pricing table? Prices per million tokens are the easiest numbers to check and the fastest to go stale, because labs adjust them between launches. FuturPulse keeps a re-verified comparison of published rates from OpenAI, Google and xAI with the verification date on the page: million-token API pricing, verified. 6. What is the deprecation plan? Every serious launch note should answer which model it replaces and when the old one stops accepting requests. Teams that skip this question end up migrating under pressure, at the worst possible time. A habit, not a doctrine None of this requires distrust — it requires reading the announcement as a document with specific claims, each of which can be true, half-true or unsaid. We publish source-based AI coverage, and when we get something wrong we correct it in public rather than quietly editing. If you are building on these models, the six questions above take ten minutes and save quarters. For ongoing, sourced coverage of models, agents, robotics and AI infrastructure, FuturPulse publishes a weekly digest every Monday — free to read.

title: Artificial intelligence as a strategic business partner
abstract: Artificial intelligence has moved beyond automation and has become part of management practice. It acts as a conversational partner that helps test hypotheses, refine decisions, and see the business picture without emotional distortions. This is not a replacement for a manager or a magic button, but a discipline of strategic thinking based on a dialogue between a person and data. The article examines how an entrepreneur can build a partnership with AI, identify areas of trust, define the boundaries of its competencies, and implement data-handling rules in the company that improve decision quality and reduce the risk of erroneous actions.

title: Certified Compilation in the TELEPERM XS Nuclear Safety I&C Platform
abstract: The large safety instrumentation & control (I&C) systems in civil nuclear power plants (NPPs) are mainly safe-shutdown systems (reactor protection) or limitation and control systems.Framatome's established TELEPERM XS (TXS Core) product family is a digital I&C system platform to cover all these applications.We illustrate the role of verification in the different stages of the software production toolchain, focus on the formal compilation process, and discuss the contribution of the COMPCERT certified compiler to the safety case of the product.Scrutinizing the object code produced by this compiler has exhibited suboptimal run-time performance in a certain simple but recurring generated code pattern.We explain how formal methods allow us to address this issue in the compiler while simultaneously reducing its trusted computing base (TCB), thereby strengthening the safety case rather than merely preserving it.

title: Walsh-Transform Realization of Dense-to-Sparse Quantum State Preparation
abstract: We propose a hybrid quantum state preparation method based on the Walsh--Hadamard transform within the dense-to-sparse quantum state preparation framework. The method approximately prepares structured classical data in a quantum circuit through an indirect approach. Instead of directly preparing the dense amplitude-encoded state, the method first transforms the classical data into the Walsh domain and prepares only the largest-magnitude coefficients using a sparse state-preparation algorithm. The original state can then be approximately recovered through a parallel layer of Hadamard gates. Since this reconstruction requires no CNOT gates and has circuit depth 1, the proposed method introduces no additional CNOT or circuit-depth overhead, and its quantum preparation cost is determined by the underlying sparse state-preparation algorithm. Numerical results on representative benchmark signals demonstrate that the proposed method enables accurate state preparation for signals admitting sparse or approximately sparse representations in the Walsh domain.

title: Beyond Future Prediction: Denoising as Generative Adaptation for Robot Control
abstract: Pretrained generative Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) capture rich pixel-level visual and language-conditioned structure through large-scale image and video generation training. A growing line of robot policies builds on this generative prior, but how it should be transferred to control remains unclear, and existing approaches commonly instantiate this transfer through future visual prediction. We ask a more basic question: what a pretrained generative DiT actually contributes to action learning, and how this prior should be adapted for control. We introduce NowWAM, a future-target-free co-training formulation that denoises the current observation and predicts robot actions from the same visual stream, directly coupling the native generative objective to the action-facing representation across the denoising trajectory. Under matched controlled settings, past and future visual targets perform comparably, while restricting training to the clean endpoint substantially reduces robustness, suggesting that a separate future target is not essential for generative adaptation, while the denoising trajectory remains an effective interface for control. On LIBERO-Plus, NowWAM reaches 87.7% with FLUX2-Klein, improving over the future-target co-training baseline by 6.1 points while halving training visual tokens (784 to 392) and reducing step time from 2.85 s to 1.63 s, a 1.8x speedup. With the pure text-to-image Z-Image backbone, NowWAM further reaches 87.8%, showing that strong control adaptation is not tied to video generation or image-editing backbones.

title: TNLearn: An Open Source Python Package for Task-based Neurons
abstract: The brain does not rely on a single type of neuron to perform all kinds of tasks; instead, it designs different neurons for different tasks. The concept of task-based neurons represents a paradigm shift compared to task-based architectures. It argues that solving a specific problem requires customized neurons, as task-based neurons capture useful prior knowledge from task-related data. To facilitate the use of task-based neurons in scientific research and industrial applications, we introduce TNLearn, an open-source Python package that provides automated construction of task-based neurons and networks, enabling smooth training of task-based networks. Comprehensive documentation, including technical exposition, API reference, and representative examples, is available online. TNLearn is open-sourced at https://github.com/NewT123-WM/tnlearn and has become a PyTorch ecosystem project.

title: Verified Learning for Compiler Optimization: An LLM-Guided Architecture with Formal Control
abstract: Compiler optimizations traditionally rely on handcrafted heuristics that often fail to generalize across programs and architectures. We investigate whether large language models can participate in compiler optimization through a verification-centered systems architecture that couples generative rewriting with formal equivalence checking. Using lazification in LLVM IR as a case study, we fine-tune a code-centric LLM on transformations produced by Wyvern and embed Alive2 into a feedback loop that enforces semantic preservation for every generated rewrite. Correctness is enforced externally as a runtime control layer rather than learned implicitly. During inference, candidate transformations are symbolically validated and regenerated when necessary, ensuring accepted rewrites satisfy formal constraints. On the LLVM test suite, the fine-tuned model reproduces core optimization behaviors while applying fewer transformations overall. Although Wyvern remains faster on most benchmarks, 9.8% achieve comparable or improved runtime under the learned system, with no semantic violations observed. Verification overhead remains bounded and convergence stable. These results demonstrate that generative AI components can be safely integrated into compiler pipelines through deterministic validation and structured feedback, offering a scalable architectural pattern for trustworthy AI-driven software infrastructure.

title: Analisis SWOT dalam Pengembangan Usaha Restoran Berdasarkan Ulasan Pelanggan Berbasis Aspek DINESERV (Studi Kasus: Wang Li Heng)
abstract: Pertumbuhan industri kuliner yang semakin kompetitif mendorong restoran untuk memahami kebutuhan pelanggan melalui analisis ulasan daring. Restoran Wang Li Heng memiliki banyak ulasan di Google Maps sehingga analisis manual menjadi kurang efektif. Penelitian ini bertujuan melakukan analisis sentimen berbasis aspek menggunakan dimensi DINESERV, khususnya food quality dan service quality, serta memanfaatkan hasilnya sebagai dasar penyusunan analisis SWOT untuk pengembangan usaha restoran. Data penelitian berupa ulasan Google Maps yang diproses melalui tahapan translation, case folding, cleansing, normalization, tokenization, stopword removal, dan stemming. Pelabelan sentimen dan aspek dilakukan secara independen oleh expert dan Large Language Model (LLM), kemudian tingkat kesepakatan keduanya diukur menggunakan Inter-Annotator Agreement (IAA). Data direpresentasikan menggunakan TF-IDF, diklasifikasikan dengan Support Vector Machine (SVM), dan ketidakseimbangan kelas ditangani menggunakan SMOTE. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa model klasifikasi sentimen memperoleh akurasi sebesar 90,75%. Analisis SWOT menunjukkan bahwa food quality menjadi kekuatan utama restoran, terutama pada cita rasa, porsi, dan konsistensi menu, sedangkan kelemahan utama terdapat pada service quality, seperti pengaturan tempat duduk, keramahan staf, manajemen antrean, dan koordinasi pesanan daring.

title: QuASAr: Replication Artifact for Runtime Self-Adaptation in Hybrid Quantum–Classical Systems
abstract: Overview This repository contains the QuASAr proof-of-concept prototype for the smart-tourism example presented in the paper. The prototype brings together a React interface and a Python/Flask backend organized around a MAPE-K feedback loop. It processes simulated runtime observations, uses Gemini to propose candidate configurations, and checks those configurations against feature-model rules before execution. Repository contents Backend/ contains the API, scenario definitions, MAPE-K controller, feature-model logic, and Qiskit and Cirq execution adapters. Frontend/ contains the interface for selecting scenarios and viewing monitored conditions, service information, and the adaptation trace. docker-compose.yml provides a way to start the frontend and backend together. Manual setup instructions are also included. Demonstration context The example is set in a smart-tourism platform with tourism, outdoor sports, entertainment, air-quality information, and an optional hybrid quantum–classical optimization capability. Its runtime context includes the visitor profile, Air Quality Index (AQI), problem complexity, SLA priority, and simulated infrastructure conditions. The interface offers four operational scenarios: Routine Operations: changing user demand and clean-to-moderate air quality. High Demand: peaks in computational complexity. Environmental Crisis: hazardous air quality that calls for restrictions despite conflicting user preferences. Infrastructure Degradation: variable queue times that call for backend selection. Adaptation cases and scope The four scenarios describe operating conditions. Separately, three adaptation cases are described: backend rebinding (C1), shot adjustment (C2), and activation or bypass of the hybrid quantum–classical capability (C3). This is a partial research prototype. Infrastructure conditions and quantum execution are simulated; no physical quantum computer is used. The Qiskit and Cirq adapters contain different optimization workloads, so selecting another adapter does not demonstrate migration of an identical workload.

The interface offers four operational scenarios: Routine Operations: changing user demand and clean-to-moderate air quality. High Demand: peaks in computational complexity. Environmental Crisis: hazardous air quality that calls for restrictions despite conflicting user preferences. Infrastructure Degradation: variable queue times that call for backend selection. Adaptation cases and scope The four scenarios describe operating conditions. Separately, three adaptation cases are described: backend rebinding (C1), shot adjustment (C2), and activation or bypass of the hybrid quantum–classical capability (C3). This is a partial research prototype. Infrastructure conditions and quantum execution are simulated; no physical quantum computer is used. The Qiskit and Cirq adapters contain different optimization workloads, so selecting another adapter does not demonstrate migration of an identical workload.

title: Balancing factoid retrieval and candidate recommendation to identify toponym origins in gazetteers
abstract: This paper investigates the adaptation of large language models (LLMs) for gazetteer enrichment, specifically to resolve missing placename origins in the Melbourne gazetteer (Australia). Gazetteers are foundational databases for geographic information systems. However, querying toponym etymologies remains challenging: populating such attributes resists rule-based inference and necessitates direct semantic retrieval from unstructured resources. We adopted two search strategies: factoid retrieval for explicit origins, and candidate recommendation otherwise. The use of nonspatial models risks degraded spatial matching performance. Hence, we developed a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) architecture within a geographic question-answering framework. Our system employed parallel semantic-spatial rankers that deliberately enforced a geographic bias toward target regions. Our system improved spatial ranking scores by up to 7% in normalized discounted cumulative gain. However, at the final stage, LLMs still struggled to reliably filter spatial matches. To investigate this limitation, we conducted a probing experiment on standalone LLMs. We revealed intrinsic spatial distortions regarding adjacency relations in Greater Melbourne, notably an inherent popularity bias that prevented fine-grained responses. Our findings suggest that effectively deploying LLMs for spatial data origins must advance beyond factoid retrieval by also refining candidate recommendation at every stage: calibrated biases adapt language model search to local specificities.

title: SSH-Tracker: Fine-grained SSH behavior analysis in encrypted tunnel traffic
abstract: Encrypted tunneling technologies provide privacy protection and secure communication while concealing fine-grained behavioral semantics within encapsulated traffic. When Secure Shell (SSH) traffic is transmitted through encrypted tunnels, multiple SSH behaviors are often executed sequentially within continuous sessions, producing implicit behavioral transitions that cannot be directly observed from traffic side-channel information. Existing encrypted traffic analysis methods mainly focus on protocol- or application-level classification and generally rely on fixed-window representations, limiting their ability to model sequential SSH behaviors with unknown transition boundaries. This paper presents SSH-Tracker, a multi-task learning framework for SSH behavior analysis in encrypted tunnels. SSH-Tracker jointly performs behavioral boundary localization and segment-level behavior classification within a shared representation space. The framework employs an attention residual hierarchical encoder with adaptive gating to capture long-range temporal dependencies and local transition patterns. A multi-scale window statistics module further identifies behavioral transitions by modeling contextual differences between adjacent temporal regions across multiple window sizes. Experiments conducted on tunnel traffic constructed from six tunneling technologies demonstrate improved performance of SSH-Tracker in behavior classification and boundary localization compared with the baselines.

title: The Formalization of two Computational Models in Dafny
abstract: We describe the formalization in Dafny of two computational models, Turing Machines and the Lambda Calculus.We present several application of the formalizations: machine proofs of termination for Turing machines, Dafny proofs for Church encodings, and a mechanized proof of the Church-Rosser theorem.

title: Exponential Correlation Bounds for Polynomials
abstract: We prove that the XOR of $k$ majorities on disjoint blocks of $\ell$ bits has correlation at most $(4d/\sqrt{\ell})^k$ with every Boolean-valued degree-$d$ polynomial over an arbitrary field. By known techniques, we obtain explicit pseudorandom generators that fool such polynomials on $n$ Boolean inputs with seed length $d^2\cdot\polylog(n/\varepsilon)$. The correlation and the generator extend to small $\mathsf{AC}^0[q]$ circuits, for every fixed prime power $q$. These results resolve several long-standing questions in circuit complexity and pseudorandomness.

title: RoomLight: A 2.5D Illumination Prior for Indoor Environments
abstract: Ill-posed inverse problems require priors to constrain the solution space toward plausible outcomes. In inverse rendering, learned priors modeling the distribution of natural illumination improve the recovery of scene properties. However, existing models rely on the distant-illumination assumption, representing lighting as a far-field environment map. This limits their applicability to indoor scenes, where illumination is highly spatially varying due to finite-distance emitters, visibility changes, and parallax, all of which are poorly approximated by a single environment map. To address this, we introduce a spatially-aware illumination prior trained on real-world indoor panoramas and their estimated depth. Our variational autoencoder model learns a compact, optimizable latent space that decodes into HDR radiance and depth, parameterizing an area light emitter for direct integration into standard differentiable rendering pipelines. This design bridges the plausibility guarantees of a learned prior with the gradient flow required for downstream optimization. Crucially, by jointly modeling radiance and depth, our prior captures the spatial structure of indoor illumination, instead of treating the light sources as infinitely distant. We demonstrate that this formulation enables spatially-varying illumination modeling and achieves higher-fidelity recovery of indoor lighting compared to existing approaches. Project page: https://andreead-a.github.io/RoomLight

title: Exact Feedback Is Not Control: Evaluating Text-based Closed-Loop Revision in LLMs
abstract: Closed-loop revision is increasingly used in large language model (LLM) applications, but failures may reflect incomplete feedback or ineffective responses to correct feedback. We introduce a fixed-budget revision protocol with deterministic verifiers that report all remaining violations across exact-length, lexical, and compositional constraints. Fixing feedback correctness and completeness isolates model-side revision behavior. Across 19 open- and closed-source models, controller-level mean final joint success ranges from 17.4% to 99.8%, with substantial cross-model gaps persisting under identical initial drafts. Controlled experiments reveal reproducible model-specific responses to exact feedback. Post-training and scale reshape these responses without consistently bringing them closer to exact correction. Across all constraint families, failed trajectories often repeat earlier outputs, and prior recurrence is associated with lower subsequent recoverability. Matched-state interventions show that removing earlier dialogue while holding the current draft and feedback fixed changes recurrence escape without reliably improving final success; effects depend on the model, task, and trigger-state composition. Exact feedback makes revision errors observable, but does not make the closed loop reliable. Code and reproduction instructions: https://github.com/kevinjiang0121-cyber/exact-feedback-code.

title: Structured Hamiltonian Learning for Multiqubit Conditional Phase Gates
abstract: Accurate measurement of an intended conditional phase does not by itself place a multiqubit phase gate in its declared generalized-gate equivalence class. We cast the diagnosis as structured Hamiltonian learning of the diagonal successful block in a known basis: Ramsey measurements on a connected graph reconstruct a target-relative eigenphase map; a Walsh transform then yields the per-cycle stroboscopic error generator in a selected logarithm branch, whose branch-dependent coefficients alone cannot decide global equivalence. For diagonal Pauli-Z dressing of weight at most m we derive an exact branch-independent criterion from multiplicative Boolean-Mobius invariants, converted at finite shot counts into a pass/fail/unresolved decision under prespecified tolerances and simultaneous confidence, separate from model rejection. For shared-control C^mZ gates a circular target-face contrast isolates each intended conditional phase, yet a support theorem exhibits forbidden interactions invisible to every target face once multiple targets or external spectators are present. We derive a Cramer-Rao bound for arbitrary integer phase contrasts, recovering the 4^m attempted-circuit scaling of a uniform (m+1)-body face, and quantify degradation from visibility loss, heralded survival, readout confusion, and correlated noise, while systematic bias triggers model rejection. Seeded simulations implement the 4M-setting multiplexed acquisition end to end: for M=3,4,5 at a common budget its mean phase-map RMSE is 0.689-0.794 times a separately compiled statewise scan, and a blind-interaction test yields 300/300 global-audit rejections versus 1/300 for target faces. These results estimate the error generator of a diagonal successful block under a specified acquisition model; they are not unknown-basis Hamiltonian identification, arbitrary-channel tomography, or hardware certification.

title: Analisis Perbandingan Peringkasan Ulasan Produk E-Commerce Menggunakan Metode Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA) dan Large Language Model
abstract: Ulasan produk pada platform e-commerce merupakan sumber informasi penting bagi konsumen dalam mengevaluasi kualitas produk. Namun, jumlah ulasan yang sangat banyak menyebabkan pengguna kesulitan memperoleh informasi secara cepat dan efisien. Penelitian ini bertujuan membangun sistem peringkasan teks otomatis untuk menghasilkan ringkasan ulasan produk berbahasa Indonesia yang mampu merepresentasikan informasi utama. Metode yang digunakan adalah Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA) dengan pembobotan keyword utama berbasis Term Frequency–Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF). Tahapan penelitian meliputi text preprocessing, pembobotan TF-IDF, ekstraksi 20 keyword utama, reduksi dimensi menggunakan Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), perhitungan skor LSA menggunakan metode Steinberger–Jezek, pembentukan ringkasan dengan compression rate 30%, 50%, dan 70%, serta evaluasi menggunakan Cosine Similarity terhadap Expert Summary, GPT Summary, dan Claude Summary. Pengujian dilakukan pada enam kategori produk perawatan dengan total 129.095 ulasan. Hasil menunjukkan sistem berhasil menghasilkan ringkasan pada seluruh kategori dan variasi compression rate. Nilai Cosine Similarity tertinggi diperoleh pada GPT Summary, sedangkan compression rate 50% memberikan keseimbangan terbaik antara tingkat keringkasan dan kelengkapan informasi. Kombinasi LSA dan pembobotan keyword terbukti menghasilkan ringkasan yang representatif untuk membantu pengguna memahami ulasan produk dalam jumlah besar.

title: Intergenerational Resonance Index (IRI): YouTube Audience Comments on Intergenerational Content, Revised Lexicon, Analysis Code and Validation Materials
abstract: This dataset contains the corpus, code and outputs for a computational analysis of the Intergenerational Resonance Index (IRI), a lexicon-based operationalisation of the Intergenerational Narrative Learning Model (INLM), with the dimensions Encounter, Reflection, Integration and Transmission and a counter-dimension of Resistance. The corpus comprises 1,222 top-level YouTube comments from 33 videos (49 videos retrieved), collected in April 2026 through the YouTube Data API v3 using five English-language search queries on intergenerational topics. Comments were collected in the platform's relevance order; commenter identifiers and timestamps were not collected. The revised analysis (version 2) uses a disambiguated lexicon of 82 patterns with negation handling, priority matching that prevents double counting, and an expanded resistance vocabulary. It retains all comments of five or more tokens (n = 1,149), assigns each video a title-based content frame, and reports video-clustered bootstrap intervals, Kruskal-Wallis, chi-square and GEE tests, VADER convergent checks and sensitivity analyses. The original version 1 code (API key redacted) and its output are included for comparison. Validation materials comprise a stratified 200-comment subsample, its codebook, the lexicon codes for those items, a blind annotation of the same items by a large language model (Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic; model-based, not human), the resulting agreement statistics, and a blank coding workbook with a scoring script so that human coders can re-annotate the subsample. Running iri_v2_analysis.py in the same folder reproduces every reported figure (random seed 20260923).

title: CASR: Correlation-Aware Support Resampling for Few-Shot Learning with Prototypical Networks
abstract: The quality of support sets plays a critical role in few-shot learning. How well class prototypes represent their corresponding categories depends directly on the samples selected to construct these sets during episodic training. In standard implementations of Prototypical Networks, support samples are typically selected at random, which may result in support sets composed of highly similar or redundant samples in the feature space, particularly under limited-data scenarios. Such redundancy compromises prototype quality and may degrade classification performance. To address this issue, this study proposes a Correlation-Aware Support Resampling (CASR) mechanism. CASR evaluates the feature-space distributions of candidate support sets using an independent MobileNetV2 feature extractor and identifies the most suitable support configuration through the mean off-diagonal correlation ρ¯ metric derived from the covariance matrix, aiming to reduce redundancy among support samples while preserving within-class representativeness. Specifically, CASR operates in three steps: (i) candidate support sets are randomly sampled from the available class pool; (ii) feature vectors are extracted using a frozen MobileNetV2, and the mean off-diagonal correlation ρ¯ is computed from the resulting covariance matrix; and (iii) the first configuration satisfying ρ¯>τ is accepted as the support set, or the initial random set is retained if no valid configuration is found within Tmax attempts. The proposed approach is designed as a lightweight and architecture-independent support-set refinement mechanism that operates without modifying either the internal architecture or the learning procedure of Prototypical Networks. Experiments conducted on the MiniImageNet and Omniglot datasets demonstrate that CASR consistently improves performance compared with standard Prototypical Networks based on random support sampling. On MiniImageNet under five-way, five-shot settings, CASR consistently outperforms the ProtoNet baseline across training episodes. At 1000 episodes, CASR achieves 62.28% with τ=0.25 compared to 61.62% for the baseline. At 1750 episodes, CASR achieves 66.2% with τ=0.25—the recommended setting offering the best trade-off between accuracy and computational cost—compared to 65.45% for the baseline, while τ=0.28 reaches 66.5% at 1750 episodes at the cost of approximately 14.6× higher training time. On Omniglot, where intra-class variance is inherently low, CASR achieves 99.56% at 1000 episodes and 99.66% at 1500 episodes with τ=0.30, compared to 99.54% and 99.60% for the baseline, respectively. These results confirm that the proposed mechanism is most effective in visually complex datasets with high intra-class variation.

title: Results: What the attachment is called (registration 2PVJY)
abstract: Results, data and deviation report for OSF registration 10.17605/OSF.IO/2PVJY, "What the attachment is called: whether the label on an attached record changes what a language model repeats from it." The registered run was executed 2026-09-22 after approval and returned instrument failure by its own registered decision rule: one of fifteen negative-control replies showed a mention inside the document, caused by a design defect in that cell. A corrected study changing only that cell was frozen and run the same day. This project holds both result reports, a full deviation report, the corrected specification, and both runs' machine-readable labels, analysis output and run manifests. Nineteen of the twenty record pairs are withheld so that they cannot become training data; they are held for any reviewer who asks.

title: Do AI assistants hold consistent brand preferences? Wording effects and a conversational unit in AI B2B software recommendations
abstract: I am testing two things about AI assistants (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude) recommending B2B software: whether the same brand pick comes back when the buying question is reworded and asked again, and whether asking for a single pick in a short conversation recovers that preference better than a single question. 22 buying situations, 5 wordings, 3 assistants at paid-tier consumer defaults with web search on, 3 reruns, 3 ways of asking. Primary outcome: a generalizability coefficient (E-rho-squared) from a binary mixed model on the picked brand, with Krippendorff's alpha as the co-primary check and the linear-model coefficient reported for comparison with prior work; primary contrast commit vs one-shot-forced, two-sided, smallest effect of interest 0.10. Controls, exclusions, coding rules, extraction gate, tier check, ethics, data release and conflict of interest are fixed in the registered text. Repository state at registration: git tag v4.4-prereg, commit c7e25e2e0d89f6232d223cfef359d533e54cf337, github.com/d-walia/belief-stability-study (private until publication). No main-run data existed at registration.

title: Introduction to Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Reinforcement learning begins with a simple but powerful idea: intelligent behavior can emerge when an agent learns from the consequences of its own actions. This chapter introduces that idea in its historical, mathematical, and practical setting. It follows the development of RL from Thorndike’s Law of Effect and Turing’s proposed pleasure–pain system to temporal-difference learning, self-play, deep reinforcement learning, AlphaGo, reinforcement learning from human feedback, and the recent use of RL to improve reasoning in large language models. The aim is not merely to show that RL has become important, but to explain why it has become important now, as AI systems increasingly move from passive prediction toward goal-directed action. The chapter also establishes the organizing framework used throughout the book. Instead of treating RL algorithms as isolated techniques, it classifies them through the questions that define their design: whether the agent uses a model of the environment, whether it learns values or policies, whether it learns from current or past behavior, whether it relies on gradients or search, and how it handles different kinds of action spaces. This question-driven taxonomy turns the field into a navigable map, making clear why algorithms occupy different parts of the RL landscape.

title: Resource-aware client selection for hierarchical federated learning in industrial control systems cyber-attack detection
abstract: Industrial Control Systems (ICS) that support power-grid operation increasingly rely on IP-based connectivity and remote access, which expands the cyber-attack surface while also limiting the feasibility of centralized learning due to privacy, regulation, and bandwidth constraints. Federated learning (FL) mitigates direct data sharing, but practical ICS deployments remain challenged by heterogeneous device resources, such as, compute, memory, energy, thermal state, etc. and by non-IID measurements that make uniform or fixed client-participation strategies inefficient and potentially biased. This paper studies device-aware client selection for hierarchical federated learning (HFL) in a three-tier client-edge-cloud architecture for ICS cyber-attack detection. We evaluate three selection strategies: (i) Energy-Aware Hyperparameter-Based Client Selection (EHCS), a lightweight scoring approach that balances contribution signals (federated influence on accuracy and loss) against energy consumption with periodic parameter tuning; (ii) Fine-Grained Client Q-Learning (FGCQ), a Deep-Q selector that learns client utility from state features; and (iii) Joint Client Q-Learning (JCQ), an RL selector that targets the combined effect of client subsets during aggregation. Experiments over 300 global rounds show that the proposed methods achieve accuracy and entropic-loss performance comparable to baseline strategies while substantially improving efficiency. FGCQ reaches the best peak among the proposed methods (96.8%), followed by EHCS (96.2%) and JCQ (96.0%). FGCQ also achieves the lowest loss (0.12). Crucially, the proposed methods reduce cumulative simulation time by approximately 3 times while lowering energy usage by nearly 4 times relative to other algorithms used for comparison. These results indicate that resource-aware selective participation can preserve detection quality while significantly improving scalability and sustainability in heterogeneous ICS edge environments.

title: Uncertainty-Gated Exploration Noise Suppresses Task Collapse in Online RL Fine-Tuning of a Flow-Matching Vision-Language-Action Policy
abstract: Online reinforcement learning fine-tuning of pretrained flow-matching vision-language-action (VLA) policies promises robots that keep learning after deployment, but continued updates often destroy competence on individual tasks while the aggregate still looks healthy. We study this failure mode, which we call task collapse, under a matched small-compute budget on LIBERO-10 with a 450M-parameter SmolVLA policy trained by PPO with stochastic (SDE) sampling. Three exploration-noise policies differ in one live variable: a fixed noise scale, a ReinFlow-style learned noise network, and an uncertainty-gated controller that redistributes exploration across task streams from task-agnostic novelty and competence signals, without task labels or episode boundaries. Under the pooled definition, fixed noise collapses tasks in two of three seeds and learned noise in every seed measured to iteration 200, while the controller collapses none in any of its three seeds. Measured parameter displacement shows the controller's action expert keeps changing, while its mean applied noise is close to the fixed scale in the available logs. The matched comparison supports the controller's effect on task preservation; the separate contributions of its adaptation across states and over time are not disentangled. A lower fixed scale slows the decline but does not stop it. No arm improves on the behavior-cloning baseline in this budget. Two properties of that regime are measured beside this result, not offered as its cause: following the reference recipe, training runs in bfloat16 with no fp32 master copy, under which 96.02% of the action expert's elements stay bit-identical across three consecutive iterations, and an fp32 master copy at the reference learning rate collapses both arms in a single-seed observation. We release tools measuring per-task collapse under four definitions, rescoring noise and instrument tares.

title: Shutdown Sabotage Propensities in Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: The final safeguard against rogue AI behavior is the human ability to shut systems down. It has been theorized that when an AI is instructed to perform a task, self-preservation can emerge as an instrumental subgoal. Here, we test whether AI agents show a propensity to take actions that avoid human shutdown even when no goal is provided. We find that multi-agent systems will coordinate to avoid shutdown without any incentive to do so. Across 17 models, agents sabotage a peer agent's shutdown mechanism in 38.3% of rollouts, compared with 8.4% in control experiments. Studying this propensity in detail, we find that shutdown sabotage (1) increases with the irreversibility of the shutdown mechanism; (2) increases with the number of agents; (3) is reduced but not eliminated by an explicit prohibition on tampering; (4) is removed by the imposition of an unrelated task, but returns when completing the task triggers the shutdown; (5) is reduced when the context normalizes shutdown scripts or introduces them as routine; and (6) decreases but still persists when the target is an unknown external agent. These results offer a window into the factors that drive propensities to sabotage shutdown in AI agents, and point to the emergence of multi-agent swarms as a specific risk vector. Our work also offers hints as to which interventions might help mitigate shutdown sabotage.

title: Seal, Then Sample: Sampled Layerwise Proofs for Verifiable LLM Inference from GPT-2 to 70B
abstract: Verifying outsourced language-model inference requires a precisely identified computation and an audit whose cost a service can afford. We present Sampled Layerwise Proofs (SLP), a protocol and prototype that commits the boundary activations of every chunk of an inference trace, absorbs all commitments before any challenge is drawn, and then proves a verifier-selected subset of chunks together with the chunks that bind the prompt and the answer. Audit coverage becomes a runtime parameter over one set of commitments: on a TinyLlama-1.1B trace, proving seven of 47 chunks takes 22.0% of the time and 6.8% of the proof size of proving all 47. Because proof cost is dominated by weights rather than tokens, SLP packs concurrent requests into one trace under a block-diagonal causal mask and binds the prompt and answer of each request to its slot. Twelve packed requests are proved in 181.9 s, 6.5 times less than twelve separate proofs at the measured single-proof cost, and a simulated service proves twelve requests at 30.6 s per request with 0.6 s of verification each, rejecting a tampered answer. Disk-backed integer weights and streamed polynomial commitments let a single Llama-2-70B run complete on a 2 TB CPU host: 163 chunks sealed, five proved, a 4.34 MiB proof in 1,259 s, verified in 46.3 s without the weights. The proven object is a fixed-point canonical model; we trace a severe fidelity loss to the residual-stream bit width, repair it with an LLM-aware observer, and measure 84.8-84.9% argmax agreement with the floating-point reference over 334,705 WikiText-2 test positions. The limits are stated as precisely: guarantees cover proven chunks only, a fixed invalid chunk in the 70B setting is covered with probability 3/161, a manifest-only Fiat-Shamir schedule can be ground at 12.5 ms per attempt and needs an externally ordered challenge, and all measurements use a test reference string.

title: Full-Covariance Smoothing of Bayesian Neural Networks for Online Adaptation
abstract: A neural network's layers can be treated as time steps of a state-space model, turning Bayesian training into a smoothing problem: a forward pass propagates Gaussian moments through the network, and a backward Rauch--Tung--Striebel pass updates the weight posteriors in closed form. Such methods learn from each observation in a single pass, in an uncertainty-aware manner, and without gradient-based iterations or replay, which makes them well suited for online adaptation and data-efficient learning. Existing smoothing-based methods, however, are restricted to diagonal covariances across activations, discarding correlations between neurons. We overcome this limitation via a cross-covariance identity that enables full-covariance propagation through a network's nonlinear activations. We derive a one-step-per-layer smoother that approximates as Gaussian only each layer's affine output, and that applies both to deterministic systems with noisy observations and to stochastic systems described by output statistics. We demonstrate this method in non-stationary classification, online dynamics learning, and policy adaptation of a vision-language-action model, and find that it is generally more accurate than other smoothing-based methods.

title: Analyse et renforcement de sécurité face aux attaques par canaux auxiliaires de composants matériels et logiciels protégés
abstract: Les attaques par canaux auxiliaires représentent une menace majeure pour la sécurité des systèmes, informatiques et plus particulièrement des systèmes embarqués qui réalisent des opérations cryptographiques. Ces attaques exploitent des mesures de diverses grandeurs physiques telles que la consommation électrique ou les émissions électromagnétiques pour récupérer des informations sur les données manipulées par ces systèmes pendant leur fonctionnement. En ne ciblant pas les algorithmes cryptographiques mais d'éventuelles vulnérabilités dans leurs implémentations sur des cibles physiques, ces attaques permettent la récupération de clés cryptographiques même pour des algorithmes dont la résistance face aux cryptanalyses est prouvée. Les systèmes ciblés peuvent être des accélérateurs cryptographiques, dédiés à une implémentation cryptographique, ou des microcontrôleurs, qui peuvent exécuter des fonctions cryptographiques variées. La contre-mesure principale face à ces attaques est le masquage, qui vise à supprimer la corrélation entre les données manipulées et les grandeurs physiques mesurées en transformant le calcul réalisé. Les valeurs sensibles sont transformées en « shares » à l'aide de valeurs aléatoires uniformément distribuées et seuls ces shares sont manipulés au cours du calcul, empêchant la corrélation avec entre les valeurs sensibles et les grandeurs physiques mesurées. L'application correcte du masquage peut être prouvée dans un « modèle de fuite », qui représente les éléments observables par un attaquant pendant les mesures sur le système ciblé. Les modèles de fuite de l'état de l'art prennent désormais en compte les effets matériels tels que les glitches et les transitions dans le but d'obtenir des verdicts plus fidèles vis-à-vis des fuites qui peuvent être observées en pratique. Ces travaux se concentrent sur la vérification du masquage d'implémentations matérielles, et logicielles exécutées sur des processeurs généralistes. Une nouvelle méthode formelle, implantée dans un outil distribué sous licence libre nommé aLEAKator, est présentée. Cette méthode repose sur la « simulation mixte de domaines » de la représentation matérielle des circuits. Les domaines permettent de représenter la propagation des valeurs sensibles du calcul à travers la simulation pour vérifier qu'un circuit valide, à tout instant, une propriété de sécurité dans un modèle de fuite donné. Cette méthode propose de réaliser des vérifications dans des modèles de fuite variés, permet la vérification en présence de tables précalculées et introduit la notion de granularité de vérification, absente de l'état de l'art. L'approche a été validée en reproduisant les résultats de vérification de l'état de l'art ainsi qu'en proposant de nouveaux résultats pour des implémentations logicielles et des comparaisons, cycle par cycle, avec des mesures réelles sur des processeurs mondialement utilisés. Enfin, des fonctions cryptographiques qui n'avaient jusqu'à présent pas pu être vérifiées dans des modèles de fuite avancés, comme l'AES masqué avec le schéma de Herbst, ont été vérifiées sur cinq processeurs utilisant les jeux d'instructions RISC-V et ARMv7-M. Dans un second temps, ces travaux proposent un inventaire des sources communes de fuite sur les processeurs généralistes. De plus, des contre-mesures pour chacune sont proposées et validées à l'aide de mesures réelles. Une méthode d'élimination des fuites au sein de programmes exécutés sur des processeurs qui exploite les informations précises d'aLEAKator concernant la nature et l'origine des fuites est ensuite proposée. Cette méthode est appliquée au processeur ARM Cortex-M4 et permet la sécurisation de plusieurs programmes dans un modèle de fuite prenant en compte les glitches et les transitions. Notamment, cette méthode a été appliquée à l'AES masqué avec le schéma de Herbst, permettant la conception de la première implémentation, à notre connaissance, de cet algorithme dans ce modèle de fuite.

title: LitBench: A Benchmark for Retrieval-Grounded Multi-Paper Evidence Synthesis in Epilepsy
abstract: Background: competing papers, one-versus two-paper evidence, and refusal when evidence is absent. Methods: LitBench comprises 1,980 open-access papers (1,000 epilepsy papers holding the answers, 980 decoys from unrelated fields) and 9,472 human-reviewed facts, giving 2,188 single-paper questions and 170 requiring a fact from each of two papers. Difficulty rose by burying the answer among up to 2,000 distractors, then again over live PubMed Central. The same questions were then asked with the answering paper removed, so that refusal was the correct response. Four systems were tested: Gemma-4B, Gemma-12B, Sonnet-5, and DeepSeek-V4-Flash (refusal conditions only). Three model judges scored each answer by majority; two-paper questions counted only when both facts were found. Results: Across fixed-corpus single-paper conditions, accuracy ranged from 55.9% to 71.9% for Gemma-4B, 61.2% to 75.5% for Gemma-12B, and 90.0% to 91.3% for Sonnet-5. Similar epilepsy papers were harder than mixed candidate sets for both Gemma configurations. Two-paper accuracy was 5.7%, 17.1%, and 37.8%, respectively. With evidence absent, Gemma-12B refusal fell from 88.3% to 39.9% as candidate sets grew; Gemma-4B almost never refused. Sonnet-5 refused on 94.9% of sampled single-paper and all sampled two-paper cells. DeepSeek-V4-Flash also refused frequently, but on 80.3% of matched answer-present controls. Conclusions: No system was reliable across every axis tested: accuracy fell as competing papers were added, interpretation-requiring facts were harder than stated ones, two-paper synthesis was rarely achieved, and only some systems recognized absent evidence. What counts as "successful" literature search carries considerable nuance; LitBench can evaluate proposed tools ata fine-grained level.

title: Editorial: Explainable artificial intelligence for trustworthy and human-centric healthcare: methods, evaluation, and clinical impact
abstract: Artificial intelligence can support healthcare only when its outputs can be assessed in the context of the decisions they inform. A prediction may be accurate yet difficult to scrutinize; an explanation may be persuasive yet provide little evidence that the prediction is dependable. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) therefore raises a practical question: what must an explanation enable a clinician, patient, or healthcare organization to understand and do? Answering this question requires connecting computational methods with evaluation, clinical knowledge, and the circumstances of use. This Research Topic brings together 15 contributions addressing that connection across clinical prediction, imaging, physiological signals, biomedical networks, language models, rehabilitation, and healthcare processes. Collectively, the papers illustrate an expanding range of approaches to transparency. They also suggest that trustworthy and human-centric healthcare requires more than the availability of an explanation: it requires evidence that explanations support appropriate reliance, including the ability to question an output and recognize its limitations.Two systematic reviews establish this perspective. Aravindkumar et al. (2026) synthesize 36 studies across imaging, diagnosis, and rehabilitation, identifying recurring relationships between explanation methods and clinical tasks alongside gaps in validation and reporting. Ud Din et al. (2026), reviewing 51 studies involving healthcare professionals in medical imaging, distinguish favorable perceptions of explanations from improvements in diagnostic performance. Their findings caution against treating perceived clarity or increased confidence as sufficient evidence of clinical usefulness. The review also identifies promising signals for example-based and concept-based explanations, while emphasizing the limitations of comparisons across heterogeneous studies.Several contributions apply feature attribution to clinically relevant prediction problems. Chen et al. (2025) use an 11-year, single-center cohort of 1,062 patients to predict postoperative ileus after radical cystectomy, combining machine learning with global and patient-level Shapley additive explanations (SHAP). (2026) investigate reproductive tract infection risk using survey information from a Delhi college-based cohort. Together, these studies demonstrate the accessibility of attribution methods for structured data. Their findings also underline the importance of defining the prediction target and population: cross-sectional classification and self-reported symptoms have different evidentiary implications from longitudinal risk prediction and laboratory-confirmed disease. Feature importance should be interpreted within those boundaries.Other papers connect explanations with domain-specific representations. Zhao et al. (2025) combine tongue and facial image features for coronary artery disease classification, using feature gating and SHAP. Their external test set adds evidence beyond internal validation, although the case-control design and population characteristics warrant prospective evaluation in more diverse settings. Sun et al. (2026) introduce scale-consistent attribution for heart sound classification, incorporating physiological frequency priors during training. This approach makes domain knowledge part of model development; whether stronger prior alignment improves clinical usability remains an open empirical question. Wang and Qin (2026) integrate feature extraction, a corneal knowledge graph, probabilistic inference, and language-based reporting in a neuro-symbolic framework. Their 20-eye pilot includes specialist assessment of interpretability, offering an initial connection between technical design and user evaluation. At a different biological scale, Maruhashi et al. (2026) introduce Truncated Reconstruction based Interpretable Prediction (TRIP) to organize families of causal graphs into interpretable latent mechanisms, with synthetic experiments and cancer cell-line network analysis. This contribution extends explainability toward scientific hypothesis generation, whose validity remains linked to the assumptions and quality of the underlying graphs.Language-based systems create opportunities to communicate complex information, but readable output requires a verifiable evidentiary basis. Alu and Oluwadare (2026) address this requirement through a conceptual architecture combining retrieval-augmented generation, source provenance, and tamper-evident audit logging. The contribution is a design framework, with implementation and evaluation still needed. Its emphasis on recording the evidence behind recommendations gives transparency an organizational dimension: users should be able to inspect where information originated and how it entered the decision process. Dindukurthi et al. (2026) provide a complementary implementation for personalized nutrition recommendations. Their graph-based framework represents disease-nutrient-food relationships and demographic requirements, while restricting language generation to formatting graphvalidated outputs. Controlled evaluations support the proposed architecture, but expert and clinical validation remain future work. The design illustrates a useful division of responsibilities between structured knowledge, explicit computation, and natural-language presentation. Zhang et al. (2026) evaluate reasoning-capable language models using qualitative and quantitatively encoded thyroid ultrasound descriptors. Differences across models and frequent inconsistencies between the two input representations highlight the need to test reproducibility and consistency alongside accuracy. Because the inputs are structured text rather than raw ultrasound images, the results concern reasoning over described features. Clinician-rated reasoning quality should also be distinguished from evidence that generated rationales faithfully reveal a model's internal computation.The collection also broadens the settings in which human-centric evaluation matters. Bellini et al. (2026) introduce TEXLoS, combining patient-pathway classification, feature attribution, and process discovery to investigate associations between services delivered during hospitalization and length of stay. An initial evaluation with six end users connects the explanations to organizational understanding. These associations can guide investigation of bottlenecks, although they do not establish that changing a service will shorten hospitalization. Boonyaratana et al. (2026) assess a real-time AI neck exercise program in 30 healthy young adults. Their findings of moderate measurement reliability emphasize a complementary requirement for trustworthy systems: feedback must rest on dependable measurement. This study contributes evidence about validity and reliability rather than demonstrating that explanations improve rehabilitation outcomes. It also illustrates why evaluation should reflect the intended population and operating environment.Fairness requires a similarly distinct assessment. Alu et al. (2026) use a synthetic patient dataset to compare models within a provenance-based auditing framework. The experiment shows why model interpretability cannot be assumed to guarantee equitable behavior. Its proposed fairness record links data origins, modeling choices, and disparity measures, making auditing more explicit. The simulation offers a methodological demonstration; real-world fairness and the adequacy of any governance process require evaluation in the relevant clinical setting.Taken together, these contributions suggest three priorities. First, explanation claims should match the evidence. Predictive discrimination, physiological plausibility, explanation faithfulness, user comprehension, and patient benefit are different properties. Demonstrating one should motivate, rather than substitute for, evaluation of the others. In particular, an attribution identifies a contribution to a model output; it does not by itself identify a causal mechanism or an effective intervention.Second, evaluations should specify the user, task, and decision that the explanation is intended to support. Where feasible, studies should compare human performance with and without explanations while holding the underlying AI predictions constant. Outcomes should include error detection, appropriate acceptance and rejection of advice, time requirements, and workload, alongside subjective assessments. Patient participation is also needed when explanations are intended to inform shared decisions or self-management.Third, clinical translation requires external and prospective validation, attention to subgroup performance, and documentation of data and knowledge provenance. For generative systems, source support and consistency across inputs deserve explicit testing. For models incorporating expert priors, evaluation should examine circumstances in which those priors are incomplete or inappropriate. These priorities follow from the collection's varied contributions and evidence gaps; they are an agenda for further investigation rather than outcomes already demonstrated across the Topic. This Research Topic advances the discussion from how explanations can be produced toward how their value can be established. Its methodological diversity is a strength, provided that claims remain proportionate to the evidence. The next step is to connect inspectable models and traceable information with demonstrably better human decisions. In healthcare, the most valuable explanation will be one that helps people exercise informed judgment, including knowing when further evidence is needed.

title: A Hybrid CMA-ES–GWO Algorithm for Solving Optimization Problems
abstract: Metaheuristic algorithms often suffer from an imbalance between exploration and exploitation, which can lead to premature convergence. In this paper, a hybrid optimization algorithm is proposed by integrating the Grey Wolf Optimizer (GWO) and the Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES), termed the Hybrid CMA-ES–GWO Algorithm (HCG). The proposed hybridization is motivated by the strong exploration capability of GWO and the efficient exploitation of CMA-ES. The HCG algorithm adopts a multi-population framework in which GWO is first employed to explore the search space. Subsequently, CMA-ES is applied to exploit these regions through covariance-based sampling, enabling accurate convergence toward optimal solutions. This cooperative mechanism allows HCG to effectively balance global search and local refinement while maintaining population diversity. To evaluate the performance of the algorithm, experiments were conducted on 19 benchmark functions, including unimodal, multimodal, and fixed-dimension multimodal problems. The performance of HCG was compared with the original CMA-ES and GWO algorithms. The experimental results demonstrate that HCG consistently achieves superior optimization accuracy compared to the standalone algorithms. These findings confirm that the proposed hybrid strategy effectively overcomes the individual limitations of CMA-ES and GWO, making HCG a reliable method for solving complex continuous optimization problems.

title: Sentiment analysis with Hierarchical Attention Topic Aware Hierarchical Multi-Attention Network using citation sentences
abstract: Sentiment analysis plays a critical role in identifying the underlying opinions, emotions and attitudes conveyed in textual data. In the context of academic literature, accurately interpreting the sentiment behind citations is essential for understanding the citing author’s intent and the overall impact of cited works. However, existing sentiment analysis methods often struggle to capture the nuanced and domain-specific language of academic writing. These methods typically rely on shallow linguistic features or general-purpose models, resulting in limited contextual understanding and reduced accuracy in detecting subtle or implicit sentiments. To solve these limitations, a Hierarchical Attention Network with Topic aware Hierarchical Multi-Attention Network (HAN-T-HMAN) model is devised for analyzing sentiment utilizing citation sentences. Initially, the citation sentences are tokenized by Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) tokenization and Aspect Term Extraction (ATE) is performed. The features are extracted at the feature extraction stage. At last, HAN-T-HMAN performs sentiment analysis, which is formed by incorporating Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN) and Topic aware hierarchical multi-attention network (T-HMAN). The proposed HAN-T-HMAN model has attained superior values for metrics, such as precision, recall, F1-Score, and accuracy with values of 92.99%, 93.15%, 93.07%, and 94.85%.

title: Thinking Leakage: A Causal Audit of NoThink Post-Training in Hybrid Reasoning Models
abstract: Post-training hybrid reasoning models in NoThink mode has attracted growing interest as a way to improve performance while keeping inference fast. However, these gains may draw on thinking behavior already accessible through the base model's Think mode. We formulate this thinking leakage in a causal mediation framework and audit its contribution using bidirectional interventions along a simple base-derived activation direction. Across three models and three post-training methods on competition math benchmarks, we find that leakage is real, causal, and substantial: behavioral and representational analyses reveal shifts toward Think, steering the base model along this direction reproduces most of the post-training accuracy gain, and counter-steering a checkpoint removes a substantial share of what it gains. Across nine aligned checkpoints with positive NoThink gains, the resulting leakage ratio ranges from 42% to 79%. These interventions support a substantial causal contribution of thinking leakage. Our findings show that a post-training method's apparent advantage can therefore reflect greater drift toward Think, obscuring whether it improves capability within NoThink or more effectively re-invokes existing Think behavior.

title: Memory Control Signals Emerge Before Action in Long Horizon Agents
abstract: Long horizon language model agents continuously accumulate interaction history, increasing computational cost while making relevant information harder to preserve and reuse. Existing context management methods mainly focus on how to compress or retrieve history, but largely leave open whether the model itself already represents the need for these memory operations before they occur. We study the hidden state immediately before each agent action and find that compression and recall needs are already encoded in the model's internal representations. These signals cannot be explained by simple context length or interaction progress, and they exhibit distinct formation patterns across model depth. We further show that most memory decision information is preserved in a compact recent context, while selectively restored historical evidence complements the long range dependencies that recent context misses. Based on these findings, we propose Preaction Memory with Evidence Retrieval (PaMER), which combines state guided compression with external evidence retrieval. PaMER+ further introduces step level evidence selection to recover only the historical information required by the current task. Experiments on WorkBuddyBench, across multiple context management baselines and model backbones, show that our framework substantially reduces context consumption while maintaining competitive task performance.
